articles.title: India-EU FTA timeline brings MedTech tariff relief closer for hospitals - Medical Buyer
articles.summary: India-EU FTA timeline brings MedTech tariff relief closer for hospitals  Medical Buyer
articles.full_text:
India’s healthcare sector now has a clearer view of when lower-cost European medical equipment and medicines could reach its hospitals and supply chains. The India-European Union Free Trade Agreement, announced on January 27, 2026, is expected to be signed before the end of 2026 and could come into force by March or April 2027, once approval and ratification procedures are complete on both sides.
The timeline matters for healthcare procurement teams because the EU is a major source of advanced medical technology for India. European exports to India already include medical and optical instruments alongside machinery, transport equipment, and chemicals, and the agreement is designed to cut both tariffs and administrative barriers on this trade.
Deep cuts on equipment duties
The most consequential provisions for hospitals and diagnostic providers concern capital equipment and devices. Indian import duties on medical and surgical equipment, which currently run as high as 27.5 percent, would fall to zero across 90 percent of the relevant tariff lines. For high-value purchases such as imaging systems, surgical platforms, and critical care equipment, the removal of duties at that level would materially lower landed costs. 																
															
Medicines and device inputs are also covered. Indian tariffs on European pharmaceuticals and chemicals, currently as high as 11 percent and 22 percent respectively, would move to zero, along with duties on plastics and related industrial inputs used in device components. The input-side cuts are relevant to domestic manufacturers that source specialized polymers and chemicals from Europe for consumables and device housings.
The scale of import dependence gives these changes added weight. India relies on imports for a large majority of its medical devices, with estimates placing that share at 70 to 90 percent, which means tariff reductions flow quickly into hospital budgets, tender pricing, and distributor margins.
Export opportunity for Indian drugmakers and device makers
The benefits run in both directions. The agreement opens access to a USD 572.3 billion EU pharmaceuticals and medical-devices market and includes liberalized tariffs for India-made medical devices intended to accelerate growth in the sector. Europe remains a large but under-penetrated destination for Indian drugmakers, with the EU accounting for about 19 percent of India’s pharmaceutical exports despite India’s position as a leading global supplier of generic medicines. 																
															
Market access, however, depends on more than tariffs. European regulatory requirements for medicines and devices remain demanding, and Indian manufacturers will need certification, quality systems, and documentation aligned with EU standards to convert lower duties into actual sales. Exchanging information on product standards and pricing ahead of implementation has been identified as an early step for companies on both sides.
Approval process and the road to 2027
The agreement is now in its final institutional stretch. The European Commission submitted its proposals on September 11, 2026, and Council approval would clear the way for signing, after which the European Parliament must give its consent and India must complete its own procedures. Negotiations stretched over nearly two decades, though most of the final progress came in the past 13 months. 																
															
The wider trade relationship provides a substantial base. Bilateral merchandise trade between India and the EU stood at USD 136.54 billion in 2024-25, with Indian exports of USD 75.85 billion and imports of USD 60.68 billion.
The agreement also sharpens a policy balance for India’s MedTech sector. Healthcare providers and procurement bodies stand to gain from lower landed costs on European equipment as tariffs phase down, creating a trade-off between import substitution goals and near-term affordability. Domestic makers of devices, consumables, and diagnostics are likely to face sharper price competition from European suppliers, even as the same agreement widens their access to one of the world’s largest healthcare markets.
MB Bureau
